#5587. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," said Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction."

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy

The researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life."

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

This variation is important because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray said. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships."

Like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's important to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict."

Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she said. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions."

Materials provided by University of Mississippi. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5585. Unpacking the implications from CMS' latest proposed Medicare Advantage changes

Unpacking the implications from CMS' latest proposed Medicare Advantage changes" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Late last week, the Trump administration released a proposed rule that includes a slew of technical changes in Medicare Advantage for 2028, citing enhanced competition as a key goal.

Analysts dove into the beefy regulation and projected that changes to MA's star ratings program would likely cull more than $100 billion in federal spending over the next decade.

Per a note from Leerink Partners, estimates from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services suggest that the changes would cut federal spending by $11.5 billion in 2031 and $107 billion through 2037.

The Leerink analysts estimate that about 58% of Medicare Advantage contracts would see lower scores using the newly proposed methodology, with about 20% of contracts losing quality bonus payments, which are tied to star ratings performance.

In the rule, CMS proposed moving to a set of 15 measures to determine the star ratings scores, which are focused on member experience and outcomes. The proposed rule would also eliminate the Reward Factor, and in tandem, these changes "would remove a cushion for contracts sitting at the critical QBP threshold, while concentrating performance across fewer measures," according to the Leerink report.

The analysts said that the potential impact of these proposals "reminds us just how many plans have been living at 4 stars for years with the hugely important Reward Factor."

The report estimates that the changes to the star ratings, if finalized, would have an uneven impact on insurers. For example, Humana would see the number of contracts earning four or more stars decline from 95% to 82.9%. Clover Health, meanwhile, would likely maintain 100% of its contracts, earning at least four stars.

UnitedHealthcare, by comparison, could see a drop from having 67.9% of its contracts in plans with at least four stars in 2027 to just 8.8% under the new methodology. For Aetna, the Leerink analysts project a decrease from 70% to 0%.

Given the scale of the changes, the Leerink analysts write that the rule sets the stage for a significant overhaul of the policies and rules that govern Medicare Advantage. The proposal is "almost overwhelming in size, scope and the impact on the industry."

Molly Turco, a policy analyst at TD Cowen, wrote in a note Monday that the proposed rule "is more significant than expected, in both revenue impact and scope and touches most core aspects of MA."

"It appears CMS aimed to reform long-standing concerns, especially Stars, in a way that takes money out of the program, while also loosening regulation on things like agents/brokers, seamless enrollment, network adequacy, etc. to help the program grow," Turco wrote. "However, we think these growth/deregulation policies are unlikely to offset the headwinds for MA."

She noted that while most of the most painful changes wouldn't impact plans until 2031 at the earliest; the delay does suggest CMS may be comfortable including more significant short-term changes to risk adjustment in the forthcoming 2028 Advance Notice, which is expected in January.

Ryan Langston, an equity research analyst at TD Cowen, wrote in the note that the proposed rule would likely be net negative for insurers with large, multi-state contracts and more people enrolled with plans earning at least four stars.

The delayed timeline of at least four years does grant plans time to adapt, Langston wrote, but the financial impacts would likely force benefit changes. The proposed rule could also spook investors concerned about what's included in the 2028 rate notice, he said.

"The combination of a smaller measure set, elimination of reward factors and reduced improvement measure protection likely lower Star ratings across the industry and force plans to mitigate lost revenue via benefit revisions," Langston wrote.

The Leerink analysts wrote that health plans are almost certain to fight the regulation. Lawsuits have become commonplace in the stars space, with multiple payers suing the feds over the most recent round of scores.

"We believe a lot of what has been proposed will change and/or not be implemented at all," they wrote. "Expect industry litigation."

#5584. 5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

#5583. Industrial internet of things satellite platform Myriota raises $40M to scale its constellation and expand

Australia-based Myriota Pty. Ltd., a global satellite platform for the industrial internet of things, today announced it has raised $40 million in the first portion of its Series C to launch next-generation satellites and accelerate customer adoption across international markets.

Main Sequence Ventures, Hostplus and Australia’s National Reconstruction Fund Corporation co-led the round. Funds SA joined as a new investor. The round raised the company’s total funding to more than $107.5 million, and is expected to close in early 2027.

Founded in 2015, Myriota’s platform makes satellite connectivity commercially viable for large-scale industrial IoT, using the same core technology to track mining equipment and trailers to also monitor fuel tanks, livestock water supplies and off-grid solar.

The company’s platform combines satellite connectivity, low-power devices, field installation tools and fleet management software to support existing infrastructure. The objective is to provide access to communication tools that connect what is in place with turnkey service, so a company can connect devices, machines and smart sensors no matter how remote they are.

“We’re at the beginning of a fundamental shift in industrial IoT,” Chief Executive Ben Cade said. “Industries increasingly rely on data from the field to make decisions about their operations, assets and resources, and as AI moves into the physical world, that data becomes even more essential.”

The company expanded its platform over the past 12 months with the launch of HyperPulse, a global 5G non-terrestrial network, or NTN, and terrestrial service, and AssetHawk, a rugged, long-life asset tracker designed to make it economical to track industrial objects.

Alongside the expansion, it also grew into new verticals such as industrial fuels. It monitors and tracks fuel deployments across North America and Latin America, with EMEA and Asia Pacific to follow.

Myriota competes in a sector led by established operators such as Iridium Communications Inc., Orbcomm Inc. and Viasat Inc., alongside a growing field of providers pursuing cheaper, standards-based connections for industrial sensors and trackers.

The company said it intends to use the funds to expand its space infrastructure, including developing and launching its next-generation satellites.

#5582. Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

An international research team has developed a new technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease. In experiments involving mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms, the approach significantly improved movement problems without requiring permanently implanted electrodes.

The technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain. When exposed to an external magnetic field, these particles generate tiny forces that activate nearby nerve cells. Unlike conventional brain stimulation treatments, which rely on surgically implanted electrodes, the new approach uses magnetic forces to influence brain activity. The findings, published in Advanced Science, come from researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), RWTH Aachen, and the Universities of Maastricht (the Netherlands) and Leuven (Belgium).

Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants

Parkinson's disease develops as brain cells responsible for producing dopamine gradually break down. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that plays a vital role in controlling movement. As its levels decline, communication within the brain's movement circuits becomes disrupted, contributing to tremors and other motor difficulties.

For some patients, deep brain stimulation can help control these symptoms. This treatment uses a device known as a brain pacemaker, which is implanted beneath the collarbone and connected to electrodes placed deep inside the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical stimulation to a region called the subthalamic nucleus (STN for short), helping to modify abnormal activity in the brain circuits responsible for movement.

Although this treatment can provide substantial relief, it requires a complex surgical procedure and does not work for everyone.

"The procedure is relatively complex, however, and not always successful," explains Prof. Dr. Danijela Gregurec from the Department of Chemistry and Pharmacy at FAU. "This puts many Parkinson's patients off, and not all patients are suitable candidates for one of these pacemakers."

The researchers believe magnetic stimulation could eventually provide another option, allowing doctors to influence the same deep brain structures without leaving electrodes permanently implanted.

How Tiny Magnetic Particles Stimulate Brain Cells

The new technology takes advantage of the ability of certain nerve cells to detect physical pressure and mechanical forces.

"We use magnetic nanoparticles that we implant in the brain," Gregurec explains. "They have a special shape and a magnetic structure. They were developed in order to transform magnetic fields into tiny mechanical forces."

Rather than sending electrical pulses directly into the brain, the technique uses these particles to produce extremely small physical movements when a magnetic field is applied.

"The traditional method establishes an electrical connection to the brain," she says. "In contrast, we use the neurons' natural mechanosensors to influence regions deep within the brain."

The process works by gently changing the shape of nearby nerve cell membranes. Imagine pressing a finger against an inflated balloon and creating a small indentation in its surface. The magnetic particles produce a similar effect on a microscopic scale.

This slight deformation opens specialized channels in the cell membrane that respond to mechanical pressure. Once opened, these channels allow electrically charged particles called ions to enter the nerve cells, changing their electrical activity and providing a way to stimulate the targeted brain circuits.

Magnetic Brain Stimulation Improves Movement in Mice

To investigate whether the technology could relieve Parkinson's symptoms, the international research team conducted experiments using mice with damage to the same types of dopamine-producing nerve cells affected by the disease in humans. This damage caused movement difficulties resembling those seen in Parkinson's patients.

"Together with our partners from Maastricht, we injected magnetic nanoparticles developed here at FAU into the animals' subthalamic nucleus," Gregurec explains. "That is the very region in the brain that is also an important target for conventional deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease."

The researchers used precise stereotactic injection techniques to deliver the particles to the intended location. These methods rely on carefully calculated three-dimensional coordinates to guide instruments into specific brain structures. Accurate placement was particularly important because the treatment needed to affect the correct neural circuits involved in movement.

After the particles were positioned, the researchers applied an external magnetic field. The results were encouraging: the mice showed significant improvements in their movement deficits.

"The effect is roughly equivalent to what we would have expected after implanting a brain pacemaker," says Gregurec.

The findings suggest that magnetic nanoparticles could provide a different way to achieve some of the benefits of conventional deep brain stimulation, without the need for permanently implanted electrodes.

Could Future Parkinson's Treatments Use Magnetic Headbands?

Another encouraging finding involved how the brain responded to the implanted particles over time. The magnetic nanoparticles remained in place throughout an observation period lasting several months, and the researchers found no signs of inflammation. This suggests that the particles were well tolerated during the experiments.

However, delivering the particles still required an injection directly into the brain. Gregurec and her colleagues are now investigating ways to make the procedure even less invasive.

One possibility is to develop particles that could be injected into the bloodstream and then travel into the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier. This protective boundary normally prevents many substances circulating in the blood from entering brain tissue. Finding a way to deliver the particles across it could eliminate the need for direct brain injections.

The researchers are also exploring compact wearable devices capable of generating the magnetic fields needed for stimulation. One possibility is a headband that patients could put on themselves, potentially making treatment more convenient and adjustable.

These ideas remain at an early stage, and the researchers expect that several more years of development will be needed before the technology could be considered for clinical use.

"Nevertheless, we are convinced that the new method has enormous potential," Gregurec states. "It is not only considerably simpler and cheaper than a conventional brain pacemaker, it is probably also more flexible. Adjusting the parameters of the magnetic field would allow us to control the nanoparticles more accurately."

Beyond its potential medical applications, the technology could also become a valuable scientific tool. By allowing researchers to stimulate nerve cells through carefully controlled mechanical forces, it offers a new way to explore how physical changes at the cellular level influence brain activity.

Although the treatment has so far been demonstrated only in animals, its ability to improve movement without permanently implanted electrodes represents a promising step toward new approaches to Parkinson's disease and brain stimulation.

WASHINGTON — A new website launched by the Trump administration provides centralized access to more than 92,000 public records from the Department of Health and Human Services and the agencies it oversees — including partially redacted entries from health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s calendar.While many of the records were previously available, the health department heralded the launch of the site as a sign of its “radical transparency.”

#5579. HHS: Medicaid state-directed payment savings 'primarily' stem from slowing growth

HHS: Medicaid state-directed payment savings 'primarily' stem from slowing growth" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Rural hospitals claim a relatively small portion of the state-directed payments being squeezed in coming years by 2025’s H.R. 1, with much of the legislation’s projected spending reductions the result of holding funds for those hospitals from growing beyond fiscal year 2025 levels, Department of Health and Human Services policy heads wrote in a new report.

The analysis, released Monday, paints a softer picture of the rate limits Republicans imposed on a supplemental Medicaid payment stream in last year’s broad budget reconciliation law, also referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act or the Working Families Tax Cut Legislation.

Hospitals and other healthcare industry groups, as well as advocates and Democrats, have said the law’s billions in projected savings—from state-directed payment changes as well as other policy areas like Medicaid work requirements—are likely to devastate providers already operating at thin or negative margins.

Specifically, the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE)’s analysis showed that an estimated 7.8% of Medicaid state-directed payments reached rural hospitals in FY2025, or $11.5 billion out of $148.3 billion. That rate is slightly above rural hospitals’ 7% share of total Medicaid hospital spending for that same fiscal year, as estimated by the CMS Office of the Actuary.

Scaling from that baseline in line with H.R. 1’s multi-year payment rate phasedown, with some cumulative adjustments, showed that total nominal cumulative spending on rural state-directed payments would decline by 42.9%, or $81.6 billion, from 2026 through 2035 under the bill. This rate is again slightly higher than the CMS Office of the Actuary’s 40.8% estimate for all affected hospitals, which ASPE said is the result of the higher average dollar weighted payment rates rural hospitals currently receive, “which means that rural providers have more room to reduce rates to meet the new limits of 100% to 110% of Medicare.”

The ASPE report’s bottom line, however, is that $75.2 billion of the $81.6 billion reduction rural hospitals face, or 92.1%, reflects projected increases over the FY2025 baseline of $11.5 billion. The remainder, about 7.9% of the projected change, is a reduction below FY2025’s estimated state-directed payments to rural hospitals.

HHS, in a release highlighting the report’s findings, said that the language used in government reports describing the full $81.6 billion 10-year spending reduction as “savings” misses the government’s primary goal of capping future growth.

“Counting every dollar of projected savings as a cut below existing funding gives the public the wrong picture. Most of these savings are not reductions below what the program spent in 2025,” HHS Chief Economist and Chief Regulatory Officer Casey Mulligan, who was one of the report’s coauthors, said in the release. “They reflect future spending increases that will no longer occur. Our analysis makes that distinction clear.”

H.R. 1’s multi-year scale down in state-directed payment rates is set to begin in 2028, and are expected to slash some hard-hit states’ Medicaid spending by up to a quarter of their total annual Medicaid spending, per one analysis. Hospitals have broadly criticized the policy changes while spending much of this year adjusting their operations to contend with the future limits supplemental revenue, expectations of increased uncompensated care costs and year-to-year expense pressures like wage and supply inflation.

Additionally, CMS earlier this year proposed state directed payment caps substantially more extensive than what was outlined in H.R. 1 and used as the basis for Monday’s ASPE report. That proposal would extend rate limits beyond the bill’s four outlined service areas (inpatient hospital services, outpatient hospital services, nursing facility services and qualified practitioner services at an academic medical center) to “all [state-directed payments]s for all services in all states.” Hospital groups have flatly opposed the proposal, which more than triples the 10-year estimated savings.

Lawmakers last year, when seeking votes, blunted H.R. 1's funding reductions for rural hospitals by inserting a five-year, $50 billion rural health fund into the legislation. Those funds have come with usage restrictions for states and providers, with critics also noting transparency concerns and the fund's relatively small scale compared to the bill's total projected impact on hospitals.

#5578. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5577. Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain

Popular medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, may have effects that extend beyond weight loss and blood sugar control. These drugs also influence biological processes involved in brain function, raising questions about whether they could help preserve memory and thinking abilities.

To examine this possibility, researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen reviewed the existing scientific evidence at the invitation of the journal Science.

Studies involving animals suggest that GLP-1 medications can influence learning and memory. However, research involving humans has produced less consistent findings. Analyses of patient health records have found an association between GLP-1 treatment and a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes. These observational findings are encouraging, but they cannot determine whether the medications themselves are responsible for the lower risk.

More definitive results have also raised questions. In Novo Nordisk's EVOKE and EVOKE+ clinical trials, semaglutide failed to slow the progression of early Alzheimer's disease. Although the treatment affected several biological markers associated with Alzheimer's, those changes did not translate into a measurable slowing of the disease.

Why Weight Loss Drugs May Still Benefit the Brain

Despite the disappointing Alzheimer's results, researchers believe GLP-1 medications could still offer cognitive benefits to certain groups of patients.

People living with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience difficulties with attention, planning, and the speed at which they process information. These cognitive problems are often associated with metabolic health and blood vessel function, suggesting they may respond differently to treatment than the changes caused by Alzheimer's disease.

Improving blood sugar regulation, metabolism, or vascular health could potentially help preserve cognitive abilities, even if the same medications cannot slow an established neurodegenerative disease.

Stina Börchers, the review's first author and a researcher affiliated with both the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen, emphasizes the need to determine whether starting treatment earlier could make a difference.

"We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit," says Stina Börchers.

Unlocking New Treatments to Protect Memory

A central unanswered question is how GLP-1 medications might influence the brain. Their potential cognitive effects could result from improvements in metabolic health, direct actions within the brain, or a combination of both.

Understanding these mechanisms could help researchers identify which patients are most likely to benefit and potentially lead to medications designed specifically to support memory and other thinking abilities.

Christoffer Clemmensen, the review's senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity treatments to explore the connection between metabolism and the brain.

"Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function," says Christoffer Clemmensen.

The researchers are calling for clinical trials that evaluate memory, attention, and other cognitive abilities beginning when patients first start treatment. Following these changes over time could help establish whether GLP-1 drugs genuinely protect brain function and clarify who might benefit most.

They also stress that treatment is not without potential drawbacks, particularly for older adults and people who are physically frail. Rapid weight loss can lead to a reduction in muscle mass, which may weaken physical function and offset some of the possible benefits.

Careful monitoring will therefore be essential as researchers investigate whether today's weight loss and diabetes medications could eventually provide new ways to protect the brain.

#5576. Despite stalling in court, Trump restrictions on foreign students have had a chilling effect on enrollment

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

West Coast Biotech & Life Sciences Reporter

Jonathan Wosen is STAT’s West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. You can reach Jonathan on Signal at jwosen.27.

Even as judges have blocked visa restrictions and other limits on foreign scholars and scientists, the Trump administration is winning outside court. New data show a clear drop in the enrollment of international graduate students, a key piece of the U.S. biomedical workforce.

That paradox was on full display last week. On Nov. 16, a federal judge issued a final ruling blocking a proposed four-year cap on how long international students and postdoctoral researchers can remain in the country. The next day, a judge in a separate case issued a preliminary injunction preventing the administration from narrowing eligibility for a work authorization program widely used by foreign students.

To student advocates like Fanta Aw, CEO of the nonprofit NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the rulings represented two wins in two days. “I’ve always believed that our judicial systems are strong and are very much still in play, and I felt relieved,” said Aw, whose organization is a plaintiff in both cases. “Our members, and in particular our students, I felt, were vindicated.”

But data released the same day as the ruling in the visa time limit case paint a less celebratory picture. A survey of more than 800 U.S. institutions conducted by the Institute of International Education found that foreign student enrollment for the current academic year has decreased 9% overall compared with 2025, with a 15% drop among newly enrolled students and graduate students. While IIE won’t have complete data until next year, the preliminary numbers suggest this will be the third consecutive year graduate enrollment has dropped — with the largest year-to-year decrease in at least 20 years, according to historical data from the nonprofit.

That trend extends to biomedicine, where foreign students make up nearly a quarter of life science Ph.D. graduates, according to new survey data from the Association of American Medical Colleges. A poll of 37 AAMC member institutions showed that the number of international students starting biomedical Ph.D. programs has decreased by about 30% since 2024, more than twice the 14% overall decline in matriculation in these programs.

The growing body of data as well as STAT’s interviews with students and immigration experts suggest that, despite the legal losses, the Trump administration’s policies on immigration have had a chilling effect on students considering coming to the U.S., and on those who are already here. Meanwhile, enrollment of foreign students is rising at some Asian universities, and experts warn that these opposing trends could jeopardize the nation’s biomedical preeminence and that it could take years to repair the loss of trust from students who no longer see the U.S. as a welcoming destination.

“People are looking at us from overseas, going, ‘We don’t really recognize this country,’” said Elizabeth Goss, an immigration attorney based in Boston. Even if Democrats’ new majority in Congress prevents further restrictions, she added, “I think we have a lot of ground to make up.”

When contacted for comment, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote in an email that the agency’s records don’t support the decline reported by IIE, though it didn’t say whether its own data show lower enrollment by foreign students, and that President Trump should be credited for cracking down on rampant visa fraud.

“Institute of International Education’s ‘reporting’ is completely misleading and not backed up by any real evidence,” the DHS spokesperson said. “So far, [the Student and Exchange Visitor Program] has not experienced a 9% drop of foreign student enrollment.”

A recent independent analysis by the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration  of the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System, a DHS database that has for more than 20 years monitored foreign students, found that international student enrollment declined by 6.3% between October 2025 and October 2026.

Concerns that the Trump administration would make it difficult for foreign scientists to enter or stay in the U.S. preceded the president’s inauguration. Since then, the administration has enacted travel bans affecting dozens of countries; instituted “extreme vetting” for visa applicants, including the review of social media profiles; and revoked more than 8,000 student visas. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has also stepped up enforcement of alleged visa violations, including the recent detention of a Princeton neuroscience Ph.D. student who had been traveling home after presenting at a scientific meeting.

But many of the administration’s efforts to more tightly regulate international scholars have not come to fruition. That includes the attempt to end “duration of status,” a policy that for nearly half a century allowed students and postdoctoral researchers to stay in the U.S. for the length of their training. DHS’s proposed four-year cap would likely have forced the vast majority of new foreign life science students to apply for extensions to stay in the country given that, on average, it takes five to six years to earn a biomedical doctorate. But a federal judge found that the proposal violated the Administrative Procedure Act, a law that governs how agencies implement new regulations.

The Trump administration has also proposed a $70,000 fee for a popular work authorization program meant to give students professional experience; academic institutions would be expected to pay the fee. And DHS is attempting to revive plans to institute a $100,000 fee for H1-B visas, which are often used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as biotech.

Even though these restrictions have not been enacted, they’ve left many foreign students with a clear sense that they aren’t wanted here.

“All these rules, it just made me feel like my immigration was a crime. That’s the biggest recurring feeling that I’ve had these past few years,” said a biomedical Ph.D. student at the University of Washington, who requested anonymity to speak freely. “You know what? I’m just here to study. I’m just learning, and I’m focused on my science. But it has felt very disruptive.”

There are growing signs that fear is impacting student decisions. A poll this summer from the Association of American Universities found that, while domestic student applications for U.S. Ph.D. programs went up by 3% this year, international applications fell 21%.

A more recent survey of 437 universities, including more than 200 in the U.S., found that nearly 60% of U.S. institutions reported lower graduate enrollment between August and October compared with the same period last year. Ninety percent of U.S. respondents cited restrictive government policies as a significant obstacle.

That trend isn’t unique to the U.S. The Global Enrollment Benchmark Survey found that nearly 80% of institutions in the United Kingdom, which has also instituted tougher immigration controls, reported reduced foreign graduate student enrollment. By contrast, nearly 60% of Asian universities that responded, including five Chinese institutions, said graduate enrollment had increased. It’s a shift that Aw says could have major implications for the global economy and the future of innovation.

“There is truly a global competition for talent,” she said. “China has made no secret that one of its most pressing priorities is international education and to bring as many talented students to its shores as they can from around the world. That used to be the United States.”

STAT’s coverage of the federal government’s impact on the biomedical workforce is supported by a grant from the Dana Foundation and the Boston Foundation. Our financial supporters are not involved in any decisions about our journalism.

#5575. WTW: Global health insurance costs set to rise 10.2% next year

WTW: Global health insurance costs set to rise 10.2% next year" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Global health insurance costs are set to rise by double digits in 2027 for the second straight year, according to a new survey.

WTW released its latest Global Medical Trends Survey, which estimates that the average gross cost for medical benefits will increase by 10.2% in 2027. This follows a 10.1% increase in 2026 and a 9.8% increase in 2025, according to the report.

In the United States, the cost for medical benefits is expected to rise by 10.3% on average, on par with 2026 and up from a 9.4% increase in 2025. Across regions, the highest increases are expected in the Asia-Pacific, averaging 12.6% in 2027.

The next-highest region was North America, with a projected 10.5% average increase.

The survey was conducted in June and August 2026 and includes responses from 393 insurers offering coverage across 92 countries. Just under half (49%) of those surveyed said they anticipate elevated medical and pharmacy costs to impact them over the next three years, and likely persist beyond that window.

The WTW analysts said this likely means that insurers will remain focused on cost containment and sharing measures in the near future.

"In the US, healthcare costs remain under sustained pressure from new medical technologies, specialty pharmaceuticals, and the rising use of GLP-1 therapies, alongside higher provider costs and the ongoing demands of chronic and complex conditions," said Courtney Stubblefield, strategy and specialty leader in Health & Benefits at WTW in an announcement.

More than three quarters (76%) of the surveyed insurers named new medical technologies as the leading cost drive for both medical and pharmaceutical costs. Sixty-five percent cited provider fee increases, and 45% named pharmaceutical advancements.

Cancer was the leading condition driving costs, the survey found, with 62% naming it as the top cost condition. Sixty-one percent of those surveyed said they have seen an increase in cancer diagnoses among individuals under age 40 when compared to the past two years.

However, when looking at the conditions where costs are growing the most quickly, cardiovascular disease rises to No. 1, cited by 54% of the surveyed insurers. Cancer was second on this ranking, and named by 51%, while diabetes was third at 28%.

"To manage this, employers need a multiyear, multifaceted strategy that addresses pharmacy spending and high-cost conditions—such as cancer, cardiovascular disease and diabetes—while keeping care affordable and accessible for employees," Stubblefield said.

#5574. Opinion: Washington and Beijing are building walls around biotechnology. That’s the wrong approach

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Kinch is a professor of pharmacology at Stony Brook University and the author of six books on pharmaceutical innovation.

For more than a decade, my colleagues and I at the Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology have tracked every experimental medicine that enters human testing anywhere in the world. Last December, I wrote in STAT that China had reached parity with the United States in terms of the absolute number of new drugs introduced into clinical trials each year. Starting in 2018, the rate of U.S. contributions began to stagnate. Meanwhile, in 2013, Chinese organizations had introduced about 30 new experimental drugs. A decade later, the number topped 400. And there is no reason to expect the momentum in either country is changing.

Over the past month, both governments have seemingly been moving to wall themselves off. On Oct. 16, Beijing proposed barring foreign acquisition of its companies’ proprietary cell and gene platforms. Within a week, the U.S. Department of the Treasury proposed restrictions that would bar Americans from taking equity stakes, forming joint ventures, or making limited-partner investments in Chinese biotech companies and their equipment suppliers.

The proposals from Beijing and Washington do not impact licensing. American drugmakers can keep licensing Chinese molecules, and Chinese companies may develop new medicines to sell to the U.S. and European companies.

That open door matters more than either wall. Data show that the U.S.-China contest in biotechnology is not one race but several. Restricting investment will not help America win the races it is already losing. The bigger threat to U.S. leadership is not Chinese capital. It is the erosion, at home, of the research enterprise that built America’s lead.

The Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology’s newest analysis, published in September in Drug Discovery Today, emphasizes the importance of these continued engagements. My colleagues and I evaluated the 17,000 new drugs that first entered human trials between 2000 and 2024, separating them into eight different modalities. These ranged from conventional pills to gene therapies. The convergence in the numbers of overall active ingredients that we reported last year turned out to be anything but uniform when looking at the details.

The growth by China was concentrated in a key subset of biologics. By the late 2010s, Chinese sponsors often had introduced more, and more novel, cell therapies annually than American sponsors. By the early 2020s, China had matched or exceeded the U.S. in the introduction of new monoclonal antibodies, a commercially important class of biologic drugs. China took a commanding lead in certain categories of monoclonals, such as multispecific antibodies and drug conjugates.

The U.S. still holds a larger share in two categories: nucleic acid drugs and gene therapy. Dominance in both technologies reflects tools built over decades of Western public and private investment. Examples include lipid nanoparticles that conveyed SARS-CoV2 vaccines, viral vectors, and CRISPR gene editing.

Those differences help explain why the two governments are building different walls. Beijing’s proposal shields cell and gene therapy from outside entities, areas where they have a demonstrated or aspirational determination to lead the world. Platforms must remain domiciled in China while individual products can be marketed abroad. That is a coherent industrial strategy, and it is paying off well. Chinese financial regulators report that foreign deals for Chinese biotech assets reached $120 billion through August 2026, up more than a third from the year before.

Washington’s proposal works differently. The Treasury Department proposal prevents American investors from punting on a piece of Chinese biotech and yet still allows American companies to pay for Chinese molecules. In areas where China now leads, the combined effect would seem at best to be a division of labor. As my co-author and I pointed out in our earlier STAT article, China increasingly invents and owns while American firms are more prone to take licenses, complete late stage development, and pay royalties.

Nonetheless, a decision to cut off scientific and/or economic engagement would seem detrimental to both nations.

Restriction is a defensive move. It does not put a single new medicine into the clinic. It treats “biotech” — which comprises drugs, devices, diagnostics, ag-tech, and many other areas — as one thing. Each of these competitive races is being run at different speeds and with entirely different players, outcomes, and pole positions.

The fundamental problem is the one described in our December 2025 article. American output of new experimental drugs has been flat since 2018. In our earlier study, China’s public sector, including universities and state-linked enterprises, contributed more than twice as many new drugs in 2024 as their American counterparts. All the while, the U.S. universities that built our lead in nucleic acids and gene therapy face shrinking federal research support as has been highlighted by STAT.

A competitor lacking fuel will lose the race even if regulators try to slow the opposition.

Three steps would accomplish more than walls ever can.

First, subject matter experts should take advantage of the public comment period the Treasury Department has opened through Dec. 7.

Those comments should press Treasury on several points. If it does impose restrictions, and it is not obvious that it should, they should be aimed narrowly at transfers of platforms and capabilities rather than at all investment. More clarity is also needed to address “NewCo” deals, in which a Chinese licensor takes a stake in a new U.S. company. Importantly, the regulator should set a date and objective criteria to review whether any new rules are working as intended.

Second, policymakers should prioritize and incentivize investment in areas where America leads or could lead. Nucleic acid and gene therapies depend on academic discovery and specialized manufacturing. Stable funding for proven models such as translational research by the National Institutes of Health, ARPA-H, and domestic manufacturing is the most obvious and reliable way to protect a declining margin. In cell therapy, policymakers should ask candidly why so many early trials now start in China (regulation, investment, technology, or combinations thereof), and how we might alleviate domestic hurdles.

Third, Washington should measure the race in a more nuanced way, such as by drug or disease type. The totals of new experimental drugs, such as those we have previously emphasized, can hide more meaningful long-term outcomes, such as FDA approvals as well as market and public health improvements. Federal agencies could start by tracking first-in-human trials by drug type and sponsor country. As this will take time, it should become a long-term indicator, ignoring annual variations. Policy aimed at the aggregate and/or based solely on short term measures will miss key details.

Walls are what you construct when you think you are under attack or are losing. In the technologies that will define the next generation of medicines, from RNA drugs to gene editing, American institutions still lead. The biggest threat does not come from abroad but from changes in domestic policy, such as cutting biomedical research. Our current lead in these fields was built with reliable investments by the public and private sectors, not barriers.

Michael S. Kinch is a professor of pharmacology at Stony Brook University and the author of six books on pharmaceutical innovation.

#5573. Why obesity affects men and women differently may be hiding in their fat

Scientists at the University of California, Riverside have uncovered a surprising difference in how the immune systems of males and females respond to obesity. Their findings suggest that certain immune cells found in body fat can help protect against inflammation and metabolic problems, while others may make these harmful effects worse.

The discovery centers on eosinophils, immune cells best known for their involvement in allergies and asthma. In experiments with mice, researchers found that these cells behave differently depending on biological sex, potentially helping explain why obesity does not affect males and females in the same way.

The study, published in PNAS Nexus, was led by University of California, Riverside biomedical scientists Meera Nair and Adam Godzik. Their findings challenge the longstanding assumption that eosinophils are largely similar cells with relatively few specialized functions. The results also point toward potential new approaches for treating obesity and its complications.

Six Types of Immune Cells Found in Body Fat

To investigate the role of eosinophils in obesity, the researchers used high-resolution single-cell sequencing, a technique that allows scientists to examine gene activity in individual cells. They identified six distinct eosinophil populations in adipose (fat) tissue, each with its own pattern of gene expression and potentially different biological functions.

This unexpected diversity suggests that eosinophils play a much more complicated role in metabolic health than previously recognized.

"Eosinophils are more complex than we once thought," said Nair, a professor of biomedical sciences in the UCR School of Medicine. "Some populations can protect against obesity, and if we can identify and activate the pathways that produce these protective cells, we may find new ways to improve metabolic health."

Why Male and Female Fat Tissue Respond Differently

One of the most striking discoveries was a difference in the immune cells found in male and female mice.

Female mice possessed a protective population of eosinophils that appeared to communicate more effectively with macrophages, another group of immune cells present in fat tissue. According to Nair, this cooperation may help create a healthier environment within fat tissue and support better metabolic function.

Male mice showed a different pattern. When given a diet high in fat, they were more likely to develop eosinophil populations associated with inflammation. Their fat tissue also contained eosinophils with gene activity patterns suggesting weaker protective functions.

These findings indicate that the effects of eosinophils on obesity depend on more than simply how many of these cells are present. The particular type of eosinophil and its interactions with neighboring immune cells may be equally important.

"This means the relationship between eosinophils and obesity is not simply a matter of how many eosinophils are present," said Rebecca E. Ruggiero-Ruff, a postdoctoral researcher in Nair's lab and co-first author of the paper. "Their functional characteristics and how they communicate with other immune cells are also critical."

A Protein That May Help Protect Against Inflammation

The researchers also identified a protein called RELM alpha that appears to play an important role in maintaining the beneficial relationship between eosinophils and macrophages.

Produced by macrophages, RELM alpha seemed to help stabilize communication between the two immune cell types in female mice. This interaction may be one reason certain eosinophil populations are better able to support healthy fat tissue.

The finding builds on earlier experiments by the same research group, which showed that administering RELM alpha to mice produced protective effects. Together, the results suggest that the protein may help regulate immune activity within fat tissue and influence how the body responds to obesity.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Obesity Treatments?

Although the results offer new insight into the biology of obesity, the experiments were conducted in mice. Researchers have also detected eosinophils in fat tissue from people with obesity, but scientists do not yet fully understand what these cells do in the human body.

Nair cautioned that additional research will be necessary before the discovery can be used to develop treatments. One particularly important question is whether therapies targeting the immune system would work differently in men and women.

"A drug may not activate the same pathways or produce the same effects in males and females, particularly when it targets the immune system," said co-first author Xinru Qiu, a postdoctoral researcher in Godzik's lab. "We need to investigate sex-specific biology more thoroughly so that treatments can be optimized for different patients."

Understanding these differences could eventually help researchers design more personalized treatments for obesity and the metabolic complications associated with it.

Scientists Plan to Recreate Human Fat Tissue in the Lab

The research team is now investigating whether the protective behavior observed in mouse eosinophils can also be studied in human laboratory models.

To accomplish this, the scientists are developing three-dimensional adipose organoids. These miniature laboratory models reproduce certain features of real fat tissue, allowing researchers to examine how eosinophils interact with fat cells and other components of their environment.

The goal is to determine whether changing communication between immune cells could encourage healthier responses in human fat tissue.

"We ultimately hope to develop human adipose organoids that will allow us to investigate whether manipulating immune-cell communication can promote healthier tissue responses," said Godzik, a professor of biomedical sciences and the Bruce D. and Nancy B. Varner Presidential Endowed Chair in Cancer Research.

The findings raise the possibility that targeting specific immune cell populations, rather than treating all eosinophils as functionally identical, could eventually provide new ways to address obesity and its complications. Whether the same protective mechanisms operate in humans remains an important question for future research.

The research team also included Lauren Vance, Yuxin He, and Djurdjica Coss, who worked alongside Nair, Godzik, Ruggiero-Ruff, and Qiu.

Funding for the study came from the National Institutes of Health, the UCR School of Medicine, and the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine.

The research paper is titled "Single-cell heterogeneity of adipose eosinophils is shaped by sex and RELMα and linked to macrophage communication networks in obesity."

Materials provided by University of California - Riverside. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Healthcare growth and engagement solutions provider WebMD Ignite is bringing in OpenAI’s ChatGPT to support health systems in advertising.

WebMD Ignite Healthcare Solutions Group President Ann Bilyew told Fierce Healthcare the increasing use of ChatGPT and other tools prior to care “changes where they [health systems] need to be visible.”

“At WebMD Ignite, we’re working with OpenAI to understand what this channel adds to the investments health systems already make in search and other media,” Bilyew said. “The question we want to answer for clients is a practical one. Can ChatGPT ads help them reach people they would otherwise miss and make it easier for those people to find a provider or request an appointment?”

Bilyew, who also serves as EVP of Health, added that is how the companies will “judge whether the channel earns a larger share of a health system’s budget.”

WebMD Ignite has already begun activating campaigns, executives say, including one with a leading academic medical center involving cardiology. The initial campaign has tested creative variations, aligned messaging and more.

When it comes to protecting patient trust, Bilyew said ChatGPT labels advertisements and separates them from answers.

“OpenAI also sets eligibility requirements for healthcare advertisers and excludes personal health conversations from ad placements,” she said. “At WebMD Ignite, we bring experience on both sides. We understand how people look for care and how health systems communicate about the services they offer. That shapes the words we choose, the claims we make and where someone lands after clicking an ad.”

WebMD Ignite says it works with more than 650 health systems—including 95% of the 150 largest in the U.S.—and 80% of the 20 largest payers.

#5571. Key insights from HPE’s Q4 earnings report

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally. The selloff suggests Wall Street still prices HPE as a low-margin server vendor, even though the results describe a networking and artificial intelligence infrastructure company with demand exceeding its ability to ship.

Fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance. HPE now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 27% to 35%, with adjusted earnings of $5.05 to $5.35 per share, according to its earnings release.

I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out. Here are my four takeaways for investors and information technology leaders:

Neri explained that networking orders grew more than 4.5 times faster than networking revenue in the quarter, up from 3.5 times the quarter before, and HPE exited the year with $10.5 billion in AI backlog.

HPE doubled its networking purchase commitments over the summer and raised them again in the fourth quarter, but those components carry lead times of 28 to 40-plus weeks, so Neri expects networking conversion to pick up starting in the second quarter. Supply constraints are a better problem to have than weak demand, but they mean fiscal 2027 hinges on converting orders rather than winning them.

The Juniper Networks integration is complete, and the annual cost-synergy target has risen to $800 million, but the bigger story remains the profit mix. Chief Financial Officer Marie Myers said networking will account for more than 40% of HPE’s operating profit by the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, up from less than a quarter of revenue. AI is a major driver, with routing orders growing by triple digits as customers connect AI data centers to one another.

Security was the soft spot, which Neri called “just timing.” When I asked whether the security portfolio is where he wants it as the industry consolidates around big platforms, he argued for a different path.

“Fortinet and we have a different strategy — the convergence of security and networking — and we are taking it all the way down to the silicon level,” he said. The convergence of networking and security is underway but will take time to execute, as a considerable amount of technical debt must go through its depreciation cycle. In a greenfield situation, organizations can easily deploy a converged solution, but in a brownfield environment, it requires much more work. This is the right strategy, but it remains a “prove-it” business for HPE.

Many neoclouds rely on vendor financing and chip-backed debt, raising real concerns about who is left exposed if the buildout slows. HPE says it has stayed out, and Neri was quite emphatic about it on the briefing.

“I want to be clear: We have not financed any neocloud through HPFS, our financing arm,” he said. “We have zero exposure to any AI financing for neocloud.” HPE has likely left some revenue on the table, but it drew the line in the right place. It will sell to neoclouds, as its $1.2 billion Vultr order shows, without acting as their bank. Enterprise and sovereign customers account for the majority of its cumulative AI orders, and if the neocloud financing chain breaks, HPE’s financing arm won’t be the one holding the paper.

Training built the first phase of AI infrastructure, and Neri believes inference will build the next and will dominate demand for AI infrastructure. “I believe by the end of the decade, 80% will be in AI inferencing,” he said. “Much of that will land on-prem. Much of that will be distributed, for sure. That’s why the server business is structurally well-positioned.”

Once agents are in production, token costs become a recurring bill, and companies will want inference running alongside their own data. Those servers require far more memory and pull in storage and services, which is better business than racking graphics processing units for a hyperscaler.

Evidence of this is the interest in Helios, the Advanced Microdevices Inc. rack that uses HPE’s Ethernet switching rather than Nvidia’s proprietary interconnect. I asked Neri whether Jensen Huang’s brief departure from Nvidia Corp. had opened that door. He said interest was building before then, as customers look to diversify.

HPE shares jumped 17% on Monday ahead of the report as part of a broader AI rally, then fell about 13% in early trading on Tuesday, ending near where they started the week. I see three reasons for this.

The first is margins. Cloud & AI operating margin was 18.4% in the quarter, and HPE guided to about 14% for fiscal 2027. Reuters reported that JPMorgan analysts called margin mix the key debate for investors.

The second is pricing. Myers said higher selling prices have been the biggest driver of server growth, and she expects gross margin to moderate in the second half as AI server volumes ramp and costs rise faster than pricing.

The third is timing. HPE expects about 54% of revenue in the second half, with the ramp tied to Helios shipments, the Oracle Corp. deal, customer data center readiness and component supply. Those are fair execution questions, but they miss the shift in where HPE’s profit comes from.

On the topic of margins, the 18.4% came off an unusual stretch of favorable pricing that should not have been modeled as permanent. Neri argued the guide is still “significantly higher than any historical margin we have had in this business,” and he’s right outside the past year. A year ago, the segment’s margin was 9.3%. Margin rate also isn’t margin dollars. At 30% to 40% revenue growth, my math shows Cloud & AI adding well over $1 billion in operating profit at the midpoint.

The bears are right that price-driven server growth doesn’t warrant a premium multiple, which is why the mix matters more. The market is fixated on the segment whose margins are normalizing and ignoring the one whose margins are expanding. Adjusted earnings per share are still guided to grow by 27% to 35%, in line with revenue growth. That’s far from the margin doom-and-gloom narrative on the stock.

The back-half concern is real but manageable. Myers described the pipeline as multiples of the backlog, and Neri said the guide assumes only historical win rates against it.

Then there’s quality. HPE is guiding to about 30% growth and at least $5.5 billion in free cash flow, has no neocloud financing exposure and has already brought leverage below its target. It trades at about eight times the midpoint of its adjusted earnings guidance. “I don’t see us at a multiple that is 8 to 9x; it makes no sense whatsoever,” Neri said on the earnings call.

For old HPE, that’s true, as it’s a server vendor, but HPE is increasingly a network vendor each quarter. In fact, during our pre-call with Neri, he led with networking and spoke at length about the business before pivoting to the server business. Expect networking to continue to drive a larger share of profits.

Fiscal 2027 is an execution year. HPE must convert purchase commitments into shipments, ramp Helios and prove that networking margins can climb even as cloud and AI margins settle. I’ll be watching networking order conversion more closely than server margins. If HPE executes, today’s multiple will prove to be too low.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.
